passages.title: Listening to the Rain
passages.text:
During the rainy season, the pupils of Hillview School noticed that water often collected near the main gate. Some children hurried across it, while others took a longer dry path. One morning, their teacher, Ms Das, asked the class to observe the area from a safe place inside the school grounds. She reminded them not to walk into moving water or approach an open drain.

The class began a five-day observation project. At the same time each afternoon, a group noted whether it was raining and whether water was visible near the gate. They drew a simple table instead of trying to measure the water themselves. On the third day, they saw that fallen leaves covered part of a nearby drain.

The pupils gave their notes to the headteacher. She contacted the maintenance team, who cleared the leaves using suitable equipment. The children watched from a distance; they did not handle the waste. On the last day, less water was visible after a shower. However, the teacher said that one observation did not prove that the problem was completely solved. The school would continue checking the area.

The project showed the pupils how careful records, safe behaviour and help from responsible adults could improve a shared place.

activities.instruction: Summarise the main events and lesson of P1 in your own words. No official word limit is asserted.
activities.modelAnswer: A class safely observed water collecting near its school gate and kept records for five days. After noticing leaves over part of a drain, the pupils reported their notes to the headteacher. A maintenance team cleared the leaves while the children stayed away from the waste. The school continued checking because a single improvement was not enough to prove a lasting solution.
assessment: Captures the main situation and outcome
Selects key ideas rather than minor details

activities.instruction: Put these sentences in order using the time and reference clues.

sentences.A: Once she reached the office, she explained exactly where the branch lay.
sentences.B: After hearing her report, the teacher contacted the caretaker.
sentences.C: First, Farah noticed a fallen branch across a school path.
sentences.D: Before anyone used it again, the caretaker checked that the path was clear.
sentences.E: Rather than moving it herself, she went to the school office.
sentences.F: After the safety check, pupils could use the path again.
sentences.G: When the caretaker arrived with suitable tools, he removed the branch.
sentences.H: Once the path reopened, Farah thanked the adults for helping.

activities.explanation: Notice → report → explain → contact caretaker → remove → check → reopen → thank. The connectors and references fix the sequence.

activities.instruction: Complete this story: After heavy rain, Tanvir saw a younger pupil walking towards a flooded part of the school yard. He knew that he should not enter the water himself ...
activities.modelAnswer: Tanvir stayed on the dry path and called to the younger pupil to stop. The child heard him and came back towards the classroom. Tanvir then told a nearby teacher about the water. The teacher guided the children to a safe route and asked another adult to keep pupils away from the flooded area. Tanvir did not try to test the depth with his foot or search for a hidden drain. Later, the school arranged for the area to be checked by the people responsible for maintenance. The younger pupil thanked Tanvir for warning him. Tanvir understood that helping someone does not always mean doing a dangerous job yourself. Sometimes the best help is a clear warning and a quick report to a responsible adult.
assessment: Presents connected events and a resolution
Does not reward entering floodwater or an open drain

activities.instruction: Write a paragraph about keeping useful observation notes for a school project.
activities.modelAnswer: Useful observation notes help us remember what we actually saw. Before beginning a school project, we should decide what information we need. We can write the date, time and place at the top of a page. A table is helpful when we want to compare the same details on several days. Our words should be clear, and we should separate observations from guesses. For example, seeing yellow leaves does not tell us their exact cause. If we miss a day, it is better to mark the information as missing than to invent a result. Working in a group also requires checking that everyone understands the headings. At the end, we can use the notes to explain our findings and the questions that remain. Good records do not answer everything, but they make our thinking easier to check and discuss.
assessment: Explains the purpose of observation notes
Distinguishes observation from an unsupported conclusion
Organises ideas and uses readable language

activities.instruction: Write a dialogue between classmates about reporting an unsafe path at school.

modelAnswer.speaker: Maliha
modelAnswer.line: There is water across the short path to the gate.

modelAnswer.speaker: Joy
modelAnswer.line: Shall we walk through it quickly?

modelAnswer.speaker: Maliha
modelAnswer.line: No. We cannot see what is underneath. Let us use the dry path.

modelAnswer.speaker: Joy
modelAnswer.line: Should we tell someone about it?

modelAnswer.speaker: Maliha
modelAnswer.line: Yes, we can report it to the teacher on duty.

modelAnswer.speaker: Joy
modelAnswer.line: I will explain where the water is. Could you come with me?

modelAnswer.speaker: Maliha
modelAnswer.line: Certainly. We should stay on this safe route.

modelAnswer.speaker: Joy
modelAnswer.line: Do we need to clear the drain ourselves?

modelAnswer.speaker: Maliha
modelAnswer.line: No. A responsible adult can arrange for trained people to check it.

modelAnswer.speaker: Joy
modelAnswer.line: All right. Let us report it now.

assessment: Includes a safe alternative and a report to an adult
